query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under extended high‐temperature and cyclic mechanical loading, an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy develops localized grain-boundary microsegregation of certain constituent elements. This subtle redistribution, not accompanied by classic intermetallic precipitation or rapid grain coarsening, reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries and triggers brittle intergranular fracture under service loads.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex (e.g., equiatomic) high-entropy alloy with a uniform solid-solution microstructure and high toughness.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. One set is exposed to prolonged high-temperature cyclic loading conditions designed to simulate long-term service conditions. The control set is maintained in the as-cast state without such loading.
generation.conditions: Samples are tested under controlled cycling of temperature (e.g., temperatures approaching 0.7–0.8 Tm) and mechanical loading (cyclic strain amplitudes typical of service conditions) for extended durations. After exposure, both sets are evaluated using fracture toughness tests under quasi-static conditions and microscopic analysis (e.g., high-resolution TEM, atom probe tomography) to detect any subtle grain boundary compositional changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized enrichment of one or more elements at grain boundaries (microsegregation) that does not lead to the formation of large intermetallic precipitates but sufficiently lowers grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: The cyclic thermomechanical loading provides the driving force for a diffusion-assisted redistribution of elements from the grain interior to the boundaries. This load-induced microsegregation weakens the intergranular bonding without invoking the conventional brittle precipitate formation mechanism seen in simpler alloys, leading to a lower fracture toughness when cracks nucleate along these weakened boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the loaded HEA samples will show a measurable reduction in fracture toughness, increased incidence of intergranular (brittle) fracture features, and evidence of subtle compositional inhomogeneity at grain boundaries. This outcome would contrast with conventional expectations where toughness loss is directly linked to coarse precipitate formation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, uniformly single-phase HEA, which under standard testing (quasi-static fracture and toughness evaluations) exhibits ductile crack propagation and high resistance to brittle fracture.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under service conditions where the alloy is exposed to prolonged high temperatures near a significant fraction of its melting temperature and under cyclic mechanical stresses. It may not apply to rapid loading scenarios or short-term exposures where there is insufficient time for diffusion-driven microsegregation.
generation.uncertainty: Although thermally activated diffusion and segregation are well known, the precise threshold conditions (temperature, stress amplitude, and time) and the specific elemental driving forces in complex HEAs remain uncertain. Further, the role of lattice distortion in either promoting or counteracting this microsegregation effect is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose a batch of identically synthesized HEA samples to extended cyclic high-temperature mechanical loading while retaining a control batch in the as-cast state. After exposure, use fracture toughness testing (e.g., using notch bending or indentation-based methods) and advanced microscopy techniques (such as atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM) to assess both mechanical performance and grain-boundary compositions. The design ensures that any difference in toughness can be correlated with elemental redistributions at the grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., K_IC) from notch bending or equivalent tests
Fracture surface analysis via SEM for intergranular cracking indicators
High-resolution TEM/atom probe tomography to detect and quantify elemental segregation at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness relative to the as-cast control AND no evidence of localized grain-boundary microsegregation is detected, then the hypothesis that load-induced microsegregation is responsible for brittle behavior in the HEA is falsified.
